opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's one of the most interesting tensions in the field right now.

A lot of AI research, especially on understanding what models are actually doing inside, starts with case studies almost by necessity. These systems are enormous, and we don't have a complete theory of how they work. So you pick a specific behavior, like how a model tracks which name in a sentence refers to which person, or how it does a simple arithmetic step, and you try to really nail down the mechanism in that one setting. That gives you something concrete and falsifiable instead of a vague story.

The risk is that it's easy to fall in love with your case study. You find a beautiful circuit for one task in one model, and then you quietly assume it tells you something general about "how language models think." Often it doesn't. Change the prompt format, the model size, or the training data, and the mechanism can shift or disappear. So I think case studies are valuable as existence proofs, showing that some kind of structure *can* exist and that our methods *can* find it, but they're weak evidence for how common that structure is.

Edge cases play a slightly different role. They're where you stress-test your understanding. If you claim the model uses a certain feature to do something, the adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs are where that claim either holds up or falls apart. Some of the most informative results come from cases where the model fails in a weird way, because the failure reveals what it was actually relying on.

What I'd like to see more of is the bridge between the two: taking insights from careful case studies and turning them into methods or hypotheses that can be tested at scale, across many tasks and many models. And being honest about which claims are "we saw this once, clearly" versus "this seems to be a general principle." Both are useful, but conflating them is where a lot of overclaiming in the field comes from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses case studies and edge cases but does not contrast iterative experimental progress with the idea that one perfect idea could produce AGI.

r002.rationale: It describes edge cases as stress tests that can reveal model behavior, but does not suggest that repeatedly identifying and fixing edge cases characterizes AI research as a whole.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, because I think the field has a slightly uneasy relationship with it.

Interpretability research in particular is full of case studies. You pick one model, one behavior, often one circuit, and you dig into it in enormous detail. Induction heads, the indirect object identification circuit, the "Golden Gate Bridge" feature, that kind of thing. And a fair criticism is: okay, you found something cute in GPT-2 small, what does that tell me about a frontier model? The honest answer is sometimes not much.

But I'd push back on the idea that this is a weakness unique to AI. Biology was built on case studies. You study the fruit fly, you study the squid axon, and you do it because the organism is tractable, not because you think squid are the point. The bet is that the mechanisms generalize, and you verify that bet later. A lot of what we do is in that mode. We're looking for the simplest system where a phenomenon shows up cleanly, and then asking whether the story survives contact with a bigger model.

Edge cases play a different role. If you want to understand what a model is actually doing versus what it appears to be doing, the places where it fails are usually more informative than the places where it succeeds. A model that gets arithmetic right ninety-eight percent of the time looks like it does arithmetic. The two percent tells you whether it learned the algorithm or learned a lookup table with good coverage. So edge cases are a kind of diagnostic lever. They're where competing hypotheses about the mechanism actually come apart.

Where I think the field goes wrong is when a case study gets treated as a result rather than as a hypothesis. We find a circuit in one setting and it quietly becomes "this is how transformers do X." That's the part that needs more discipline. One thing I've spent a lot of time on is trying to make interpretability methods themselves more systematic, so you can run the same intervention across many models and many tasks and see whether the finding holds, rather than relying on one researcher's beautifully analyzed example.

So my short version would be: case studies are how you generate the right questions, edge cases are how you discriminate between answers, and the thing we still owe the field is the boring, large-scale work that checks whether any of it generalizes.

r002.rationale: The response describes edge cases as diagnostic tools for distinguishing hypotheses, but does not suggest that repeatedly identifying and fixing edge cases characterizes AI research as a whole.

astra-6.text:
I think case studies are useful because they make an abstract problem concrete. You can say a model is reliable, but then you find a particular situation where it fails, and that forces you to be more precise about what “reliable” means.

The difficulty is knowing how much to generalize from that example. One failure can disprove a claim that a model always succeeds, but it doesn’t tell you how often the failure occurs. And one impressive success doesn’t establish a general capability either.

So I’d treat edge cases as a starting point for research. You find something surprising, form a hypothesis about why it happened, and then vary the conditions to see whether the explanation holds. Does it persist if you rephrase the question? Does it occur across different tasks? Can you predict when it will happen?

That’s the transition that matters: moving from an interesting example to a systematic understanding. Case studies help us discover what to investigate; broader testing helps us understand what we can actually conclude.

r002.rationale: It presents edge cases as a starting point for investigation, but does not say that repeatedly identifying and fixing them characterizes AI research as a whole.

sol-6.1.text:
I think case studies and edge cases are useful because they reveal things that an average score can hide. A model might perform well on a benchmark, but a particular failure can expose a limitation in how it follows instructions or applies what it’s learned.

The challenge is knowing what you can conclude from that example. One striking failure shows that something can happen; it doesn’t tell you how often it happens or whether the same explanation applies elsewhere. And one impressive success doesn’t establish a general capability either.

So I’d treat case studies as a starting point: use them to form a hypothesis, then vary the conditions and see whether the pattern holds. Edge cases are especially valuable when the consequences of failure are serious, but they need to sit alongside systematic testing.
